 Peak Design is best known for its excellent travel backpacks , camera accessories and cleverly designed everyday carry gear, but the San Francisco-based brand is now turning its attention to charging accessories.
 The company has unveiled a collection of four premium charging essentials, including a magnetic power bank , a foldable wireless charging station, a slimline wall charger and a range of USB-C cables.
 It's a bold move into a category dominated by Anker and Belkin, though Peak Design isn't necessarily trying to compete on price.

 What the wattage labels really mean 
 Total output is a shared budget
 A charger’s total-wattage figure describes the maximum power available across its ports, not a promise that every connected device receives that amount. When several devices are attached, the charger’s internal power-allocation rules divide the available budget. A laptop that negotiates a high-power profile can therefore receive less when a phone, tablet or accessory is plugged in.
 UGREEN’s cited four-port listing specifies its overall rating and identifies two ports capable of the highest listed individual output. That makes the first two USB-C positions the ones to reserve for a demanding laptop or other high-draw device. The listing does not establish that all four ports can simultaneously operate at their individual maxima.
 Anker’s A2687 likewise has a total ceiling that is different from its highest single-port figure. The 150W number is a supported mode for one port, not the charger’s total rating and not the official product name. Treat it as a negotiated profile available when the connected device, cable and charger state all support it.
 Why a laptop may not draw the headline figure
 USB-C Power Delivery is negotiated between the charger and the device. The laptop requests a profile it understands, then limits intake based on its own firmware, battery state, temperature, workload and charging design. A machine advertised with a high-wattage USB-C input may still choose a lower profile with either charger. The cable also has to be rated for the requested current and power.
 For that reason, a higher single-port number is not proof of shorter charging time. It can matter when your particular laptop accepts that profile, but it does not override the laptop’s input limit or the power distribution that occurs after other devices are connected.

 Port count and simultaneous charging 
 When the four-port UGREEN layout is the better fit
 If you routinely charge a laptop, phone, tablet, watch, earbuds or another USB device at the same time, a fourth connection can eliminate a separate low-power adapter. The UGREEN listing is explicitly for a four-port model, so it is the logical choice when connection count is your first constraint. Confirm the connector types and regional configuration before ordering; the four-port listing should not be inferred from reviews of another Nexode Pro design.
 When Anker’s three USB-C ports are enough
 The A2687 is a three-port USB-C charger. That is a clean arrangement for a laptop, phone and tablet when all three devices use USB-C, and it avoids needing a USB-A cable. It is less convenient if you need four devices attached or if one of your everyday accessories still requires a different connector.
 Port count alone does not tell you the power each port will receive during simultaneous use. Before choosing, write down the devices you normally connect together and check the manufacturer’s output-distribution chart for the exact regional model. A charger that has the right number of sockets but reallocates power away from your laptop may be less useful than one with fewer ports and a distribution pattern that matches your routine.
 A practical simultaneous-use worksheet
 List the devices you charge together. Record the laptop’s required USB-C input, the phone or tablet’s preferred fast-charge standard, and any low-power accessories.
 Mark the device that must maintain performance while plugged in. This is usually the laptop, a gaming handheld or another device being used under load.
 Reserve the charger’s highest-capability port for that device. On the UGREEN listing, that means one of the two ports identified for the highest individual output.
 Check the multi-port allocation table for the exact SKU. Do not assume the single-port figure remains available after adding two or three devices.
 Choose the model whose remaining ports match your cables. A nominally powerful port is not useful if your daily accessories cannot connect without extra adapters.
 Charging protocols and cable requirements 
 UGREEN’s published protocol coverage
 UGREEN’s Nexode Pro family page says the family supports PD, QC, SCP, AFC and PPS, and describes compatibility with modern smartphones, tablets and laptops. It also mentions 45W Samsung Super Fast Charging 2.0. Those are family-level statements; they do not prove that every Nexode Pro variant exposes every protocol at every port or that every device reaches its maximum rate.
 For a purchase decision, match the protocol your device actually uses rather than counting protocol names. A laptop normally depends on USB Power Delivery, while some phones select a manufacturer-specific or PPS profile. If your phone’s fastest mode requires a particular protocol, verify that the exact four-port listing supports it on the port you plan to use.

This is a particular accessory-and-mode combination, not a general promise that any power bank will accept 150W from the A2687.
 If this use case is your reason for buying the Anker charger, verify four things before checkout: that your power-bank model is one of the compatible Prime versions, that AI Mode 2.0 is available on your device and current firmware, that the cable meets Anker’s stated requirements, and that the feature is offered in your country. A generic USB-C cable can work for ordinary charging yet fail to expose this special profile.

These features can help you inspect charging status or select a supported operating mode, but they do not change the charger’s total electrical limit. If you prefer a screen and Anker’s software-oriented controls, they are legitimate reasons to favor this model even when your raw wattage needs would be met by either charger.

Its built-in 70 cm cable and foldable pins may reduce packing clutter, but those features do not describe the four-port charger compared in the main table. Verify the variant before treating the review as purchase evidence.
 A decision process that avoids the wattage trap 
 Identify the exact SKU. Select the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 4-Port listing or the Anker A2687 listing, not a search result that combines several similarly named products.
 Count simultaneous connections. Pick four-port UGREEN if you genuinely need four connections and its confirmed connector layout fits; pick three-port Anker if three USB-C devices cover your routine.
 Check the demanding device’s input requirement. Compare your laptop or other high-draw device’s accepted USB-C Power Delivery profiles with the charger’s published port capability.
 Verify cable ratings. Use a cable rated for the requested power. For the Prime Power Bank’s special recharge mode, use the cable specified by Anker; it is not supplied with the charger.
 Review multi-port power allocation. Look at the exact regional listing and decide whether your laptop will retain enough power when the other devices are connected.
 Check regional details. Confirm plug format, electrical input range, connector configuration, stock and firmware-dependent features for your country.
 Choose features only after compatibility. A smart display, app controls or a retractable cable can improve convenience, but they cannot compensate for missing ports or an unsupported charging protocol.
 What the available evidence can—and cannot—tell you 
 The manufacturer pages establish the published output, ports, protocols and dimensions listed above. They do not establish which charger runs cooler, sustains its maximum output longer, charges a particular laptop faster, or has a lower long-term failure rate.
 No controlled head-to-head test was available for these exact products. The hands-on article covers the retractable-cable UGREEN variant rather than the four-port model, and it is not a comparison with Anker. Therefore, claims about a measured temperature winner, efficiency winner or universal charging-time winner would go beyond the evidence.
 Prices and promotions are also volatile. A current sale price, stock status or regional bundle should be checked at the time you buy rather than inferred from an older listing. The same caution applies to firmware-dependent modes and country-specific plug versions.
 Buying checklist 
 Confirm the full product name and model number, especially for the UGREEN charger.
 Verify the number and type of ports on the exact regional listing.
 Compare your laptop’s required USB-C Power Delivery profile with the charger’s port specification.
 Check the charger’s power-allocation table for the number of devices you normally connect.
 Use appropriately rated USB-C cables; do not assume every cable supports the highest advertised mode.
 If buying the Anker for Prime Power Bank charging, confirm AI Mode 2.0, compatible hardware and the required cable.
 Confirm plug format, input voltage, dimensions, weight and availability for your country.
 Keep the purchase receipt and model information so support can distinguish the four-port UGREEN unit from the retractable-cable version.
 Bottom-line recommendation

Buy the Anker Prime A2687 when three USB-C ports, its Smart Display and related controls, or the conditional Prime Power Bank recharge mode are more valuable than a fourth connection.
 If neither special case applies, choose by connector count, simultaneous-load behavior, cable availability and regional SKU—not by the largest number printed on the box. The evidence supports a needs-based choice, not a blanket winner.

 How to choose before you order
 List every device you will charge at once. Include laptops, phones, tablets, watches, earbuds, cameras and power banks. Note which use USB-C and which still require USB-A.
 Check each device’s actual input requirement. A laptop may request 65W, 100W or more; a phone may require PPS for its fastest mode. The charger’s maximum number is irrelevant if the device cannot accept it.
 Decide whether you need three or four connections. Count the ports you need simultaneously rather than counting devices you own.
 Account for shared power. If you need a high-power laptop charge while also charging a tablet and phone, inspect the manufacturer’s multi-port output table and expect the available wattage to be divided.
 Choose the exact SKU. For UGREEN, verify that the title says “160W 4-Port” if that is the model you intend to compare. Do not substitute the retractable-cable version. For Anker, verify model A2687 and the official 160W, 3-port name.
 Match the cable to the intended rate. Use a properly rated USB-C cable, and obtain the compatible cable required for the Prime Power Bank’s 150W mode if you plan to use it.
 Check the country version. Confirm plug format, port arrangement, included accessories and local availability. Product names and bundles can vary by market.

 The available UGREEN hands-on account concerns the retractable-cable model. It cannot be used as a measured performance result for the 4-port charger, and it does not compare either UGREEN version directly with A2687. Reliability, long-term failure rates and safety rankings are likewise not established by the cited material.
 Setup and troubleshooting
 A laptop is charging below its expected wattage
 Confirm that the laptop’s USB-C port accepts charging at the requested level; some USB-C ports support data or display only.
 Use a cable rated for the laptop’s required wattage.
 Disconnect other devices temporarily. Shared output can reduce the laptop’s allocation.
 Try the charger’s highest-output USB-C port: USB-C1 or USB-C2 on the cited UGREEN listing, or the port specified for the desired mode on A2687.
 Check the laptop’s charging indicator after reconnecting. A lower negotiated rate can reflect the laptop’s own thermal or battery-management limit rather than a charger fault.
 The phone does not show its fastest charging mode
 Verify that the phone supports the protocol involved, such as PPS, QC, AFC or a manufacturer-specific mode.
 Use a compatible cable and remove hubs or adapters that can alter negotiation.
 Test with only the phone connected so the charger is not reallocating power.
 Remember that family-level protocol support does not guarantee maximum speed on every handset.
 The Prime Power Bank does not recharge at 150W
 Confirm that the power bank is a compatible Prime model.
 Enable or select AI Mode 2.0 if the power bank requires it.
 Use the cable supplied for the feature or a replacement explicitly compatible with the required Anker Protocol profile.
 Connect the power bank directly to A2687 and remove other loads while testing.
 Allow the power bank and charger to reach normal operating conditions; the 150W statement is a conditional maximum, not a guaranteed constant rate.
 The charger appears to stop or restart when several devices are connected
 Disconnect all devices, reconnect the highest-priority device first, then add the others one at a time. This reveals whether a particular cable, accessory or combination is causing renegotiation. If the behavior persists with different cables and a single device, stop using that setup and contact the manufacturer rather than continuing to cycle a potentially faulty charger.
 Price, availability and regional checks
 Current sale prices and promotions are volatile, and the available specifications do not provide a comparable price check. Compare the exact SKU, included cable, plug type, warranty terms and return policy in your country instead of relying on a “160W” label shared by multiple variants.
 For UGREEN, make sure the listing is explicitly the 4-port charger if you need that layout. For Anker, look for model A2687 and the official 160W product name. If a listing calls A2687 a “150W charger,” treat that as shorthand for its supported single-port mode and verify the total-output specification.
 Verdict
 Buy the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 4-Port when your deciding factor is an additional port or the ability to draw up to 140W from either of its two specified high-output USB-C ports. Buy the Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display), A2687 when three USB-C ports meet your needs, its display and associated features matter, or you specifically use the compatible Prime Power Bank’s conditional 150W AI Mode 2.0 recharge.
 Both are 160W-class chargers, so headline wattage alone should not decide the purchase. Match the exact variant to your connectors, cables, devices and simultaneous charging plan; that is the distinction the product names conceal.

 Set the minimum laptop output. If your laptop needs 100W, either charger’s cited top port can exceed that. If you specifically need the highest supported single-port mode, Anker’s 150W figure is higher than UGREEN’s cited 140W.
 Decide whether the Anker power-bank feature applies. Verify that you own the compatible Prime Power Bank and can obtain the required cable. Do not count this feature if you are charging a different battery pack.
 Check the exact SKU and regional listing. For UGREEN, distinguish the 4-port charger from the retractable-cable model. For Anker, confirm model A2687, the local plug format, and the current port diagram.
 Review the simultaneous-output table. Use the current manufacturer chart for the exact model. If a listing does not state a value, treat it as unknown rather than assuming every port retains its solo maximum.
 Verify cable ratings. Match each cable to the intended power level and protocol, especially for charging above 100W or using Anker’s power-bank mode.
 Compare the delivered price and warranty in your region. Prices, promotions, stock, and included accessories change; a historical or promotional price is not a dependable value comparison.
 Features and everyday usability
 Anker’s display and modes
 A2687’s product identity includes a smart display, and Anker documents AI Mode 2.0 for the qualifying power-bank scenario. These features appeal to buyers who want status information or a specific Anker charging workflow rather than a basic adapter. The available specifications do not establish how the display behaves under every multi-device load or how much faster a particular laptop charges in practice.
 UGREEN’s retractable-cable convenience is variant-specific
 The reviewer’s positive observations about a built-in screen, 70cm retractable cable, and foldable pins may be useful if you are considering that separate UGREEN model. They should not be used to assume the 4-port charger has a built-in cable, the same screen, or the same port distribution. Treat retractable-cable convenience as a reason to investigate that SKU, not as a feature of every Nexode Pro 160W product.
 Size, travel, and workspace considerations

Comparable dimensions and weight for the exact UGREEN 4-port model were not stated in the cited information, so no fair size or portability winner can be declared. Foldable pins, a built-in cable, or an integrated display can change how a charger packs, but those features must be verified on the exact regional model.
 For desk use, the extra UGREEN port can reduce cable swapping. For travel, compare the charger’s measured size, plug design, cable storage, and local electrical certification rather than relying on the 160W label. A high-output adapter still needs a suitable wall outlet and cables rated for the intended load.
 What has not been established
 No controlled head-to-head test is available for these exact models. The available evidence does not establish which charger runs cooler, sustains high output longer, charges a particular laptop faster, wastes less energy, lasts longer, or offers better value at current prices. The UGREEN hands-on report concerns the retractable-cable variant, not the 4-port model used in the main comparison.
 Those gaps matter because USB-C charging performance varies with device firmware, battery state, cable quality, room temperature, and the number of connected loads. Manufacturer wattage is useful for narrowing a purchase, but it cannot substitute for a test of your own device combination.

 You need four charging connections rather than three.
 Your primary device can use the cited 140W capability on USB-C1 or USB-C2.
 You are willing to verify the exact 4-port SKU, regional plug, and current power-sharing chart.
 You do not need the Anker-specific Prime Power Bank mode.

 You want three USB-C ports and the smart-display design.
 You specifically value the supported 150W single-port mode.
 You own the compatible Anker Prime Power Bank and will use AI Mode 2.0 with the required cable.
 The published 65 × 52 × 35mm, 220g specification suits your workspace or travel kit.
 If your decision comes down only to “140W versus 150W,” the numbers are too close to settle the purchase by themselves. Count ports, identify your laptop’s actual input limit, confirm protocol and cable compatibility, and check how the exact charger allocates power with several devices attached. Those details determine which adapter will be more useful in your setup.

Ugreen's new 5-port 160W charger with display launches in the US - Notebookcheck News 
 4
 Ugreen has brought its 160W Nexode Pro Charger to the US market. Previously launched in China late last year, the charger is now available via Amazon for $89.99 . That price makes it significantly cheaper than Anker's 160W Prime charger ( curr: $149.99 on Amazon ), while also offering more charging ports. 
 Like Anker's Prime charger, the new Ugreen 160W Nexode Pro Charger offers a 160W total output and a smart display for monitoring charging status. The main differences here come down to the price and port selection. While the Anker model features three USB-C ports, Ugreen adds a fourth USB-C port and a USB-A port, allowing up to five devices to charge simultaneously.
 ⓘ Ugreen
 Ugreen 160W Nexode Pro Charger 1 
 The top two USB-C ports can each deliver up to 140W when charging a single device, which Ugreen says can charge a 16-inch M4 Max MacBook Pro to 56% in 30 minutes. With multiple devices, the charger puts out a total output of 160W shared across the five ports. Even then, one USB-C port can still provide a consistent 100W with up to three devices connected or 65W with four or five devices attached, leaving enough power for a laptop alongside smaller accessories. 
 The built-in display can show charging information such as total power output, temperature, animated emoticons, and more. At 76 × 36 × 76 mm, the charger is not the most compact option, though its foldable prongs should make it easier to pack for travel. 
 The Ugreen 160W Nexode Pro Charger is now available on Amazon for $89.99. Buyers looking for a more affordable option can also pick up the 100W version with the same five-port design for $69.99.

The number of USB ports in the device design. Note that this refers only to classical, full-sized ports — the so-called USB-A; the number of USB-C ports, if available, is specified separately (see below).

The number of USB ports (of any type) corresponds to the number of gadgets that can be simultaneously connected to the charger using adapter cables or plugs for the corresponding port. At the same time, it should be noted that not all chargers are capable of providing full power to all charging outputs at once; for more details, see "Charging Current". As for the specific number of ports (USB-A and/or USB-C), nowadays relatively simple chargers with 1 port or 2 ports are the most popular. This is because individual chargers are usually purchased for one or two specific gadgets, and a larger number of charging outputs is comparatively rarely required. Nevertheless, you can easily find models with 3 ports and even more in the market.
USB-C ports
The number of USB-C ports provided in the design of the charger.

USB-C is a relatively new type of connector; it is slightly larger than microUSB and features a reversible design that allows you to insert the plug either way. Despite its compact size, these charging ports can offer quite advanced capabilities — particularly high power delivery and various quick charging technologies. On the other hand, in gadget chargers, this type of port is noticeably less common than full-sized USB (USB-A) ports and comes in smaller quantities — one, rarely two, and as a rarity three USB-C ports. This is because detachable cables typically rely on standard USB ports, which are easier to use with removable cables, and installing such ports in a charger (even a compact one) is not difficult. Therefore, in practice, it only makes sense to specifically look for a device with USB-C if you already have a compatible cable (or a gadget with a suitable plug).
Max. power (USB)
The maximum energy level that the charger can deliver to a specific port. This parameter determines the charging speed of the gadget and the ability to power high-demand devices, such as laptops.

It's important to note that when using multiple ports simultaneously, the total power of the unit is often distributed among them, reducing the speed for each individual port. For example, a 65W adapter can deliver full power to a single laptop, but when a second smartphone is connected, it will share the resources, limiting the main port to, say, 45W. To achieve the stated maximum, it's necessary to use a quality cable, and the device being charged must support the corresponding charging power.
Power (for all ports)
The total charging power available when all ports are used simultaneously. This parameter is especially important for those who want to replace several power adapters with a single charger.

It is worth noting that the power available across all ports can even be lower than the power available from a single port. The specific power ratings of each connector are individual and depend on the model. For example, a model with two connectors may deliver 100 W through one port, while the total power may be 95 W (60 and 35 W, respectively).
Fast charge
Fast charging technology supported by the device.

By itself, fast charging, as the name suggests, reduces the charging time compared to the standard procedure. For this, increased voltage and/or current power is used, as well as a special smart process control. But the possibilities and features of such charging may be different, depending on the specific technology used in the device. The same technology must be supported by the charger too — this is the only way to 100% guarantee correct operation. However some types of fast charging are mutually compatible — this point should be clarified separately, and compatibility is not always full.

Nowadays, the following technologies are most widely used: Quick Charge of different versions (3.0, 4.0, 5.0), Power Delivery (version 3.0, 3.1, 3.2), Pump Express, Samsung Adaptive Fast Charging, Huawei Fast Charge Protocol, Huawei SuperCharge Protocol, OPPO VOOC, OnePlus Dash Charge. Features
— Operation indicator. In some models it also provides additional information about operating modes, malfunctions, etc. Most often, such a light indicator is in the form of a separate light or a clearly visible backlight system. And additional information can be provided by changing the colour of the backlight, by blinking, etc. However, even without these features, the operation indicator provides additional convenience in use. In particular, it allows you to determine whether the charger is receiving power and working normally — this can be useful when diagnosing various problems. It is also possible to use non-standard backlighting — for example, as a night light that makes it easier to navigate in an unlit room (especially since gadgets are often put on charge just at night).

— Display. Own display on the charger case. This is usually the simplest screen with a few characters, but it is enough to display various additional information that makes life easier for the user: current voltage and current values, fast charging status, error codes, etc. On the other hand, this complicates the design, but in fact such information is required less often; Therefore, very few chargers with displays are produced.

Charger connection port
Port used to connect the power cable to the charger. This parameter is indicated mainly for wireless models, including car models (see "Type"), but it can also be relevant for other varieties — in particular, individual docking stations.

In general, when choosing, this parameter does not play a decisive role: a power adapter with the appropriate plug must be supplied in the kit. However, information about the power plug can be useful when looking for a spare or replacement power source. The options here might be:

— USB-C. One of the miniature varieties of the USB connector; microUSB differs from similar in many respects primarily in its two-sided design (which allows you to connect the plug to either side), as well as in smaller sizes. Is a universal standard; in fact, this means that, if necessary, you can also power the charger from a “non-native” adapter with a USB-C cable – the main thing is that this adapter can provide enough power.

— microUSB. Another smaller version of the USB connector, earlier than the USB-C described above. It is considered less perfect, and therefore noticeably less often used as a power connector for wireless charger; one of the key differences is the one-way connector design, which is less convenient to connect. MicroUSB is also a common standard and allows the use of third-party power supplies.
